Source to Sea / Citizen Scientists

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Three adventurers and citizen scientists take to the water to measure the health of the Vaal river system from its source to where it meets the ocean...we explore their findings

Summary:
FRANZ FULS (engineer & freelance journalist from Ermelo in Mpumalanga) has teamed up with Canadian adventurer with a background in science education TROY GLOVER and Australian prospector BRETT MERCHANT to paddle from the source of the Vaal (in Breyten, Mpumalanga) to the sea (Alexander Bay, Northern Cape) to measure the HEALTH of the Vaal river.
It's the longest continuous water body in SA -- they will paddle more than 2500km. They've partnered with WESSA (WILDLIFE AND ENV SOC OF SA) and they're endorsed by numerous scientists and environmentalists. They use WESSA's methodology for testing their water samples. They call themselves "citizen scientists" and the aim of their trip is to measure the health of the Vaal which is so crucial to the survival of Gauteng and NorthWest and industry/mining/farmers along the way. On the experition they make frequent stops to speak to famers, industries and children to transfer the idea that citizen scientists can make a difference if they're better informed.

The team has been taking footage of their trip for a feature-length documentary. We can have access to that footage. The trip will end in Alexander Bay on 5 April...a team from National Geographic will join them on the last two weeks of the journey.


Further information:
In early 2013 RAND WATER commissioned a fly-over of the source of the Vaal and the Vaal Dam to survey the damage done by coal mining in Mpumalanga and acid mine drainage on the Witwatersrand as well as countless other environmental challeges to the water which they have to purify -- Rand Water may soon be forced to hike tariffs dramatically as they have to follow more steps in the purification process...and/or face watershedding much like the loadshedding we're seeing with electricity. Water outages hit some Johannesburg suburbs very hard soon after.
The Lesotho Highlands Water Scheme's second phase is slowly getting started, tenders are being awarded (Polihali Dam -- communities being moved now, it's likely to be finished in 2023) -- and when the deal with Lesotho was signed, the minister said clearly that the water would be mainly for Gauteng and further North, for mining and industry. Rand Water is being stretched more and more to provide water for muicipalities beyond its original Gauteng mandate...municipalities as far afield as Mpumalanga & Northwest have essentially run out of the capacity to service the water needs of the northern parts of the country/platinum belt/drought stricken communities.
Tragically, the pristine beautiful glorious water form the highlands all come through the tributaries of the Vaal and into the sewage pit of the Vaaldam, which -- it has been estimated by Govt itself -- will lose the capacity THIS YEAR to dilute all the salts and pollution we're thrown at it. (A massive bulk sewage purification plant that was needed a decade ago already still hasn't been completed to the south of JHB and Franz & co will tell us of rowing through raw sewage as treatment plants downstream (like Parys) struggle to cope.
So the three intrepid TRIWATER adventurers are fighting for a very very important cause -- making communities and farmers and kids along the river aware of what their options will be; how to become citizen scientists themselves...how to fight back.

Press Release:


SUGGESTED STUDIO INTRO: After 4 long years of planning and preparation three kayakers from three continents took to the water in January this year to paddle down the longest continuous water body in South Africa – their mission, more than mere adventure – they called themselves “CITIZENS SCIENTISTS”. What they wanted to do was test the QUALITY of the river water along the way to contribute to the country’s scientific knowledge about this sensitive river system. The TRIWATERS TOUR made some shocking findings about water QUANTITY along the 2500km stretch of river.

Script:


SCRIPT_SOURCE TO SEA

LEON BASSON, NORTHERN CAPE FARMER: If the river dries up, it would be over for me and my animals. For everyone living around the Orange River. If it dries up you can bury yourself because no-one on God’s earth can live without water.

GERT WESSELS, ERMELO FARMER: Since I’ve joined this land, since 90, 91, this is the first time I’ve been able to drive through in a vehicle. The level is lower than in August last year after the winter.

These are farmers that live along the Vaal and Orange Rivers. Their comments have been recorded by three citizen scientists on a SOURCE TO SEA survey of the Vaal River – from its origin in Mpumalanga, through its confluence with the Orange River…all the way to where it runs into the sea in the Northern Cape.

Franz Fuls from Ermelo on the Mpumalanga Highveld had spent years writing investigative stories and blogging on the impacts of mining on the dams, wetlands and rivers around his home – he says complaining got him nowhere. So he conceived the TRIWATERS TOUR, inviting two adventurers from Canada and Australia to share in the adventure and back him up with their skills.

JOHN WEBB: They set out to promote conservation among communities on the river – and also conducted various biodiversity monitoring projects along the way. Four years and 98 days later they are back on terra firma.

JOHN: Let’s go back the beginning. What made you embark on this project in the first place?
FRANZ: I am an industrial engineer that has turned bunny hugger for lack of a better word. I’ve had an environmentalist calling me a bunny hugger…and I saw over time living in Ermelo the degeneration of the Vaal River.
Franz roped in mining prospector Brett Merchant who’d paddled Australia’s longest river, solo, two years ago, and environmental activist and teacher Troy Glover from Canada.
The team was self-supported – no-one to help set up camp or carry the stacks of equipment they needed to paddle, sleep and upload daily media reports.
Safety training was their first order of business.
Because they get to go places that scientists rarely have the capacity to explore, Franz believes adventure sportsmen should contribute to science by collecting data in remote spots…but he didn’t quite know how to make it official – and so the Wildlife and Environment Society of South Africa helped him define his role as a citizen scientist.
JOHN LINK: WESSA is an environmental NGO whose mission is to implement high-impact conservation projects that encourages public participation in caring for the earth – they assisted the TRIWATERS TEAM in training for their expedition
JOHN: Explain about citizen science – it seems a new concept to me certainly?
CATHERINE RITCHIE, Wildlife & Environment Society South Africa: what citizen science has done is to give people an opportunity to engage with issues on a practical level and then use the info that they’ve gained from the citizen science practices to make wise lifestyle choices.
The TRIWATERS team took to the water at the source of the Vaal at Breyten, half an hour north of Ermelo on the Mpumalanga Highveld. This is where they took their first water sample, just as WESSA had taught them, using the miniSASS toolkit.
FRANZ: You take the net, you go into that area, you disturb the sand, you disturb the rocks, you pick up rocks and see if there is something living on it, you bump against the reeds and catch whatever is in there. You take all of that and you dump it into your fancy scientific tray, and you start seeing, okay what do we have here. So you go through this, does it have a shell or not, no okay it doesn’t have a shell; does it have legs, yes it does have legs, is it short stubby legs, yes, well then it must be a true fly. You go through this and you may find bugs and beetles, you may find crabs and shrimp …and you take all of this and you tick them off on the list.
BONANI MADIKIZELA: We have elderly women in Limpopo, we’ve got chiefs in KwaZulu-Natal applying this with their subjects and we really appreciate the bottom-up approach and I think everybody is going to be a scientist in this country soon.
Bonani Madikizela, ecologist and head of research at the Water Research Commission that funded development of the mini-South African Scoring System says it’s delivered valid science for two decades and requires commitment over expertise.
BONANI: It’s simple and we think it’s cost effective – people in Canada are using miniSASS, people in India are using miniSASS, they are telling us how exciting it is so we are excited about this – in fact miniSASS has won more than three awards nationally and internationally for being such a community-based monitoring tool.
WESSA linked the TRIWATERS team with communities along the way…encouraging them to adopt the river where they live. Citizen scientists’ findings are uploaded to a website and cross-checked by a national coordinator in the government’s Department of Water and Sanitation.
BONANI: We don’t want miniSASS to be just used a way of playing with nature…we want to fix the conditions and water quality in this country…
Which is what Franz has in mind too – he feels it’s everyone’s responsibility to look out for our water sources, because we’re all complicit in degrading them.
FRANZ: The first part that was an unpleasant surprise was the source of the Vaal River. Being the place where the river is born you expect it to be perfect, it was not! Just a stone’s throw above the source of the Vaal River is a relatively new municipal graveyard…so water that falls there when it rains runs through a fresh gravesite to the source and what we found at the source where fungal spikes sticking out like little fingers all over …
There’s little published science on the effect of cemeteries on water sources, but when human corpses decompose organic and inorganic decay products, bacteria and viruses seep into percolating water. It will be some months before these miniSASS findings have been analysed.
FRANZ: So we started off with the worst score you can get on river health using citizen science technology.
Although the miniSASS readings improved form here, the water level suddenly dropped – so dramatically that the team dehydrated from the effort of getting the heavy boats through dry riverbeds.
FRANZ: We had three days of dragging these heavy boats before we abandoned that we needed medical attention. So that was a shock, the goal of this was a project was around water quality and suddenly the main issue became water quantity! From the research I knew that South Africa has a great potential to become water deficit in the near future, but we were doing this in the rain season; our major risk was floods, not lack of water!
The Canadian paddler had to go home for personal reasons – Franz and Brett soldiered on alone, recording extensive eutrophication of the Vaal Dam – like red tide in the ocean, poisonous to fish and difficult to reverse where pollution continues unabated…and where there’s been far too little rain.
FRANZ: The farmers all along the Vaal River and the Orange were telling us this is the lowest the river has been in two decades.
JAPIE CILLIERS, ERMELO FARMER: Since 91 it’s been the driest year – especially now in Jan and Feb – unknown to us – heat as well – high evaporation levels…water levels in the dams are very low…it’s going to be a be a long winter
From Mpumalanga, right through Gauteng and the Northern Cape, they recorded extensive damage done by mining. But the biggest shock was that the two rivers didn’t actually meet.
BRETT: When we got to the end of the Vaal River we were pretty shocked to find out that the river stopped before the Douglas Weir – 25km short of the actual confluence to the Orange.
BRETT: From the confluence we had a daily ritual of putting sticks out along the beach where the current water level is and every morning we noticed that the river level was going down and we continued to notice big pump and irrigation channels branching off from the Orange.
Finally they had to make a devastating call…
FRANZ: The river just continues to drop man and as the team leader I’m thinking of canning this expedition…hiking in the desert through a dead river is not what we came for.
BRETT: We had to make the heart-breaking decision of breaking the kayaking off and driving the last 400 km or so – while doing water samples along the way.
BONANI: That is a very very very serious thing…remember they were doing this during the rainy season…so we need that data, we need that information…I’m sure Water and Sanitation would be very curious to get that information from Franz.

PROMO 1 = 10”
A new frontier for adventure-seekers – kayakers undertake citizen science to contribute to South Africa’s understanding of a sensitive river system.


PROMO 2 = 15”
A source-to-sea expedition by citizen scientists on South Africa’s largest river system yields shocking results – what lies behind the severe water shortage in the Vaal and Orange rivers?


PROMO 3 = 15”
Why are the Vaal and Orange Rivers so dry? Adventure kayakers-turned-citizen scientists investigate river health form the source of the Vaal to where it runs into the sea.

Water outages hit some Johannesburg suburbs very hard soon after. The Lesotho Highlands Water Scheme's second phase is slowly getting started, tenders are being awarded (Polihali Dam -- communities being moved now, it's likely to be finished in 2023) -- and when the deal with Lesotho was signed, the minister said clearly that the water would be mainly for Gauteng and further North, for mining and industry. Rand Water is being stretched more and more to provide water for muicipalities beyond its original Gauteng mandate...municipalities as far afield as Mpumalanga & Northwest have essentially run out of the capacity to service the water needs of the northern parts of the country/platinum belt/drought stricken communities. Tragically, the pristine beautiful glorious water form the highlands all come through the tributaries of the Vaal and into the sewage pit of the Vaaldam, which -- it has been estimated by Govt itself -- will lose the capacity THIS YEAR to dilute all the salts and pollution we're thrown at it. (A massive bulk sewage purification plant that was needed a decade ago already still hasn't been completed to the south of JHB and Franz & co will tell us of rowing through raw sewage as treatment plants downstream (like Parys) struggle to cope. So the three intrepid TRIWATER adventurers are fighting for a very very important cause -- making communities and farmers and kids along the river aware of what their options will be; how to become citizen scientists themselves...how to fight back.
